title: Odds form
objectives: Update odds by multiplying by the likelihood ratio
See evidence as a fixed step on the log-odds line

screens.prose: Back to 1,000 people and the familiar test. Before testing, people with the condition are outnumbered 10 to 990, which is 1 to 99.
screens.question: Among the positives, how many healthy people are there for each person with the condition?

hints.text: How many positives are healthy, and how many have the condition?
Compare these two branches.
49.5 healthy positives against 9 true ones. Divide 49.5 by 9.

feedback.correct: 49.5 against 9, so 5.5 healthy people for each true case.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the healthy positives with the true positives.

byKey.before: That is the ratio before the test, 990 to 10. Use the positives only.
byKey.flipped: You divided 9 by 49.5. That is cases per healthy person; the question asks the other way.
byKey.prob: That is a probability, 9 out of 58.5. The question asks for a ratio of one group to the other.

explain.text: Among positives it is 9 to 49.5, which is 1 to 5.5. Before the test it was 1 to 99. The test shrank the gap from 99 to 5.5.

screens.prose: A ratio like 1 to 5.5, cases to non-cases, is called the **odds**. We write odds as a fraction: $\tfrac{1}{5.5}$.
screens.question: Turn odds of 1 to 5.5 into a probability. Give a decimal.

hints.text: Out of every 6.5 positives, how many are cases?
1 case for every 5.5 non-cases makes 6.5 people. So $p = 1 / 6.5$.

feedback.correct: $1 / 6.5 = \tfrac{2}{13} \approx 0.154$, the answer from the last two lessons.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Odds compare cases with non-cases; a probability compares cases with everyone.

byKey.odds-as-p: You took the odds, $1/5.5$, as the probability. A probability divides by everyone: $1 + 5.5$.
byKey.flip: That is the chance of being healthy. You want the chance of a case.

explain.text: 1 case and 5.5 non-cases make 6.5 people, so $p = 1/6.5 \approx 0.154$. In general, odds $= \dfrac{p}{1-p}$ and $p = \dfrac{\text{odds}}{1 + \text{odds}}$.

screens.prose: The odds went from $\tfrac{1}{99}$ before the test to $\tfrac{1}{5.5} = \tfrac{18}{99}$ after a positive.
screens.question: By what number were the odds multiplied?

widget.label: Factor the odds were multiplied by

hints.text: Divide the odds after by the odds before.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the odds after the test by the odds before.

byKey.probs: You divided the probabilities, 0.154 by 0.01. The question is about the odds.
byKey.hit: That is the detection rate. Divide one set of odds by the other.
byKey.drop: You subtracted 5.5 from 99. Odds change by multiplying, so divide.

explain.text: The odds grew by 18. And $18 = 0.9 / 0.05$, the detection rate over the false-positive rate. That ratio is the **likelihood ratio**: how many times likelier the evidence is with the condition than without.

screens.prose: This line is spaced so that each step multiplies the odds by the same amount. The arrow multiplies the odds before the test by the likelihood ratio.
screens.question: Keep the ratio at 18 and slide the chance before. What does the arrow's length do?

options.text: It grows as the start moves right
options.why: Slide the start and watch both ends: they move together. Multiplying by 18 is always the same step on this line.

options.text: It shrinks as the start moves right
options.why: The probability gain shrinks near 50%, but the arrow does not. It always multiplies the odds by 18.

hints.text: Watch the two points as you slide. Does the gap change?
Both ends of the arrow move together.

feedback.correct: The same evidence is always the same step on this line.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide the start and watch the arrow.

explain.text: Each step on this line multiplies the odds by the same factor, so the evidence is always one fixed jump. The line is the logarithm of the odds, the **log-odds**. Evidence adds $\ln 18$ wherever you start.

screens.prose: A new case. You think a stock has a 20% chance of beating earnings: odds of 1 to 4. A leaked figure is 6 times likelier if it will beat than if not.
screens.question: What is your new probability that it beats? Give a decimal.

hints.text: Multiply the odds, not the probability.
Start from odds of 1 to 4.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the odds by 6, then turn the odds back into a probability.

byKey.probs: You multiplied the probability 0.2 by 6. A probability above 1 is impossible: multiply the odds instead.
byKey.lr-odds: You took 6 to 1 as the new odds. The ratio multiplies the old odds of 1 to 4.
byKey.prior: That is where you started. The leak should move you.

explain.text: Odds $\tfrac{1}{4} \times 6 = \tfrac{3}{2}$, so $p = \tfrac{1.5}{2.5} = 0.6$. On the line, the point jumps from 1:4 to 3:2.

screens.prose: A signal fires on 30% of up days and on 30% of down days. Up days are 55% of days. Today the signal fired.
screens.question: What is the chance today is an up day? Give a decimal.

widget.label: Chance of an up day given the signal

hints.text: What is the likelihood ratio of this signal?
$0.3 / 0.3 = 1$. Multiplying the odds by 1 leaves them as they were.

feedback.correct: The ratio is 1, so nothing moves.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out the likelihood ratio first.

byKey.hit: That is how often the signal fires on up days. It fires just as often on down days.
byKey.joint: That is up and firing together. Divide by every way the signal fires.
byKey.sum: You added the prior and the detection rate. Evidence multiplies odds; it never adds probabilities.

explain.text: The signal is equally likely either way, so its likelihood ratio is 1. Odds times 1 are unchanged: still 0.55. Evidence with a ratio of 1 is noise, however often it fires.

screens.prose: You give a merger a 10% chance of completing. News arrives that is 3 times likelier if the deal is on track than if not.
screens.question: What is your new probability that it completes? Give a decimal.

hints.text: Turn 10% into odds first.
Odds are $0.1 / 0.9 = \tfrac{1}{9}$. Times 3 gives $\tfrac{1}{3}$, so $p = \tfrac{1/3}{1 + 1/3} = \tfrac{1}{4}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the odds, not the probability.

byKey.probs: You multiplied the probability 0.1 by 3 and got 0.3. The likelihood ratio multiplies the odds, not the probability.
byKey.lr-post: You took the ratio 3 as the new odds, 3 to 1. It multiplies the old odds of 1 to 9.
byKey.prior: That is where you started. News with a ratio of 3 should move you.

explain.text: Odds before: $0.1 / 0.9 = \tfrac{1}{9}$. Times 3: odds of $\tfrac{1}{3}$, so $p = \tfrac{1}{4}$. Multiplying the probability instead gives 0.3, which looks plausible but overstates the news.

screens.prose: Every time you multiplied odds by a likelihood ratio. Write $\neg H$ for not $H$. The **odds form of Bayes' rule** comes from writing Bayes' rule twice.
screens.question: Put the lines in order. Start with Bayes' rule for $H$.

lines.text:
$P(
eg H \mid E) = \dfrac{P(E \mid 
eg H)\,P(
eg H)}{P(E)}$: Bayes' rule again, for $
eg H$

$\dfrac{P(H \mid E)}{P(
eg H \mid E)} = \dfrac{P(E \mid H)}{P(E \mid 
eg H)} 	imes \dfrac{P(H)}{P(
eg H)}$: divide the first line by the second, and $P(E)$ cancels
Posterior odds $=$ likelihood ratio $\times$ prior odds: name each fraction

hints.text: You need both versions of Bayes' rule before you can divide.
Bayes for $H$, Bayes for $\neg H$, divide, then name the pieces.

feedback.correct: Dividing two Bayes' rules cancels the awkward $P(E)$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write Bayes' rule for $H$ and for $\neg H$ before dividing.

byKey.o3: Dividing needs both lines of Bayes' rule first.
byKey.o4: Naming the pieces comes last, once the division is done.

explain.text: Dividing the two versions cancels $P(E)$, the hardest term to find. What is left is posterior odds $=$ likelihood ratio $\times$ prior odds. Taking logs turns the product into a sum: evidence adds on the log-odds line.

screens.prose: A trend signal fires on 60% of trend days and 40% of other days, so its likelihood ratio is 1.5. You start at odds of 1 to 4 that a trend has begun. Each signal is fresh, independent evidence.
screens.question: How many signals in a row do you need before the odds reach at least 1 to 1?

widget.label: Signals needed
widget.accept: 4. Three give odds of $0.84$; four give $1.27$.

hints.text: Each signal multiplies the odds by 1.5.
You start here, at odds of $\tfrac{1}{4}$.
$0.25 \times 1.5 = 0.375$, then 0.5625, then 0.84375, then 1.27. Count the steps.

feedback.correct: Three signals leave you short at 0.84; the fourth takes you past 1.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the odds by 1.5 once per signal until they reach 1.

byKey.round-down: Three signals give odds of $0.25 \times 1.5^3 \approx 0.84$, still short of 1. You need a fourth.
byKey.added: You added 1.5 to the odds. Each signal multiplies them.
byKey.half: Two signals give odds of $0.25 \times 2.25 \approx 0.56$, still short of 1.

explain.text: Each signal is one jump of $\ln 1.5$ on the log-odds line. You need $\ln 4 / \ln 1.5 \approx 3.42$ jumps, so 4 whole signals. A weak signal can still matter if you get it often.

ideas: Odds compare cases with non-cases: odds $= p/(1-p)$, and $p = \text{odds}/(1 + \text{odds})$.
Evidence multiplies the odds by its likelihood ratio, $P(E \mid H) / P(E \mid \neg H)$.
A likelihood ratio of 1 changes nothing; on the log-odds line every piece of evidence is a fixed step.

formula.name: Odds form of Bayes' rule
formula.tex:
\dfrac{P(H \mid E)}{P(
eg H \mid E)} = \dfrac{P(E \mid H)}{P(E \mid 
eg H)} 	imes \dfrac{P(H)}{P(
eg H)}
formula.note: Posterior odds equal the likelihood ratio times the prior odds.

summary.trap: The likelihood ratio multiplies odds, never probabilities, and it is not itself the answer.

quiz.prose: A bookmaker's odds say a horse wins 3 times for every time it loses. That is odds of 3 to 1 on.
quiz.question: What probability of winning does that imply? Give a decimal.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the wins by wins plus losses.

byKey.against: That is the chance of losing. 3 to 1 on favours winning.
byKey.third: You divided 1 by 3. A probability divides the wins by all races, $3 + 1$.

explain.text: Odds of 3 mean 3 wins for each loss, so $p = \tfrac{3}{1 + 3} = 0.75$.

quiz.prose: You start at 50% that a stock is mispriced. A screen flags it, and the screen's likelihood ratio is 4.
quiz.question: What is your new probability? Give a decimal.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the odds of 1 by 4, then convert.

byKey.probs: You multiplied the probability 0.5 by 4. Multiply the odds instead.
byKey.lr-as-p: You turned the ratio upside down. A ratio above 1 raises the odds.

explain.text: 50% is odds of 1. Times 4 gives 4, so $p = \tfrac{4}{5} = 0.8$.

quiz.prose: A fraud rule has a likelihood ratio of 10. Before it fires, the odds a payment is fraud are 1 to 50.
quiz.question: What are the odds after it fires?

options.why: You took the likelihood ratio as the answer. It multiplies the odds you had before.
You divided by 10. A ratio above 1 makes fraud more likely, so multiply.
You added 10 to the top. Odds change by multiplying.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the prior odds by the ratio.

explain.text: $\tfrac{1}{50} \times 10 = \tfrac{10}{50} = \tfrac{1}{5}$: odds of 1 to 5, a probability of about 0.17.

quiz.prose: You think a deal is as likely to close as not: odds of 1 to 1. A report arrives that is four times likelier if the deal fails: a likelihood ratio of $\tfrac{1}{4}$.
quiz.question: What is your new probability that the deal closes? Give a decimal.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the odds by $\tfrac{1}{4}$, then convert.

byKey.lr-as-p: You took odds of $\tfrac{1}{4}$ as a probability. Odds of 1 to 4 are 1 in 5.
byKey.probs: You multiplied the probability 0.5 by $\tfrac{1}{4}$. Multiply the odds instead.

explain.text: Odds $1 \times \tfrac{1}{4} = \tfrac{1}{4}$, so $p = \tfrac{0.25}{1.25} = 0.2$. A ratio below 1 is evidence against.
